doc.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Adjusting from swing to rock 'n' roll piano
summary: Hyman says his blues and boogie background helped, and describes pop-singer backgrounds with triplets.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: But what kind of adjustment was there for players who were let’s say swing oriented, to start playing that different style? Was it a big deal?

Well yes and no. As Milt Hinton used to say “yes and then again, no.” Of course there were adjustments to be made. Rock ‘n roll was a blues style basically and I knew what to do I think because I had grown up with a lot of blues and boogie woogie piano records by Meade Lux Lewis and Albert Ammons and Pete Johnson and all those people. And so it wasn’t all that remarkable to figure out how to play along with some of those people. And many of them really were blues singers. Then there was another kind of rock ‘n roll which came about soon after that. People weren’t blues singers at all. They were people like Jill Corey for example, just to name one that I remember. Pop singers, in other words, for whom it became customary to play a very formularized background. The pianist would always play triplets. High triplets that would go to Mars and back again [scats].
